question: What is needed to automate decomposition, error analysis and program repair?
asked_by: Reppert et al., Iterated Decomposition: Improving Science Q&A by Supervising Reasoning Processes
remaining_question: Can an LM revise the decomposition of a multi-step LM program, localize what causes a failure and repair it reliably enough to replace human iteration (e.g. a failed-to-success flip rate approaching a human developer's), both on tasks with automatic evaluation (where, on Who&When, the best of three attribution methods found the decisive failure step only 14.2% of the time and a trained tracer, AgenTracer-8B, only improved on frontier LLMs) and on tasks with subjective answers that have no ground-truth answers or automatic evaluation function?

blockers.name: A measurement
blockers.next: Measure how often an LM that revises a multi-step LM program's decomposition, localizes the cause of a failure and repairs it turns failures into successes, against a human developer, on tasks with automatic evaluation and on subjective tasks without it.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2408.08435v2: Automated Design of Agentic Systems
findings.claim: A meta agent that iteratively programs new agentic systems in code, conditioned on an archive of earlier designs and scored on validation data from the target domain, discovered agents that outperformed hand-designed agents, by 13.6 F1 on reading comprehension and 14.4% accuracy on math, with smaller gains on multi-task and science. The authors note the search uses only numerical evaluation results and propose, as future work, letting the meta agent analyse running logs for debugging; they add that many tasks involve subjective answer evaluations that do not have ground-truth answers and that it is also important to design novel evaluation functions in ADAS to address these tasks.
findings.setting: Experiment: Meta Agent Search, in which a meta agent iteratively programs new agents in code, conditioned on an archive of earlier designs; Reading Comprehension, Math, Multi-task and Science domains; agents scored by numerical performance results on validation data from the target domain, with no analysis of running logs.
findings.bears_on: Automatically adapting LM programs (Reppert's end state; the passages do not mention decomposition as such): a meta agent can program agents in code that outperform hand-designed agents when candidate agents can be scored numerically on validation data from the target domain; analysis of running logs for debugging (items 3-4) is not used and is named as a future direction, and the authors call it important to design novel evaluation functions for tasks without ground-truth answers. Shown only where such a numerical score exists, so it settles no part of what automation needs without one.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2406.16218v2: Trace is the Next AutoDiff: Generative Optimization with Rich Feedback, Execution Traces, and LLMs
findings.claim: Trace jointly optimised the meta-prompt and two code functions (create_prompt and extract_answer) of a DSPy-based LLM agent on Big-Bench Hard beyond what DSPy's COPRO optimizer can, especially on algorithmic tasks; in another experiment, masking OptoPrime's execution trace led to a significant decline in performance and stability. The authors state that the debugging ability and context limits of the LLM used in OptoPrime crucially determine the scale of problems that can practically be addressed today.
findings.setting: Experiment: Trace optimizing a DSPy-based LLM agent's meta-prompt and two code functions on Big-Bench Hard (15 examples for training, 5 for validation, the rest for testing), with an automatic evaluation function comparing the outputs to ground truth, compared with DSPy's COPRO; a trace-masking ablation of the LLM-based optimizer OptoPrime in a separate experiment that includes a Push task.
findings.bears_on: Reppert items 3-4 (machine-accessible tooling from result to error source to fix proposals): in one experiment, masking the execution trace from the LLM-based optimizer OptoPrime caused a significant decline in performance and stability, and the authors say the LLM's debugging ability and context limits bound the scale of problems addressable today. The Big-Bench Hard result used automatic comparison to ground truth, unlike open-ended tasks without such a check.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2505.00212v3: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
findings.claim: On the Who&When dataset of annotated failure logs, the best of three automated failure-attribution methods identified the failure-responsible agent 53.5% of the time but the decisive failure step only 14.2%, some methods were below random, and reasoning models such as OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 did not reach practical usability.
findings.setting: Benchmark evaluation (experiment) on the Who&When dataset: failure logs from 127 LLM multi-agent systems with fine-grained annotations linking failures to specific agents and decisive error steps; three automated failure-attribution methods, with the primary experiments using GPT-4o, and other open-source and closed-source models and the reasoning models OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1 also evaluated.
findings.bears_on: Error analysis (Reppert item 3): the automated failure-attribution methods tested, including with reasoning models, could not reliably localize the step causing a failure in LLM multi-agent systems.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2509.03312v2: AgenTracer: Who Is Inducing Failure in the LLM Agentic Systems?
findings.claim: The authors report that state-of-the-art reasoning LLMs score generally below 10% on agentic failure attribution, and that AgenTracer-8B, trained with multi-granular RL on trajectories annotated automatically by counterfactual replay and programmed fault injection, outperforms Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-4-Sonnet on Who&When by up to 18.18% and gives feedback that improves MetaGPT and MaAS by 4.8-14.2%.
findings.setting: Experiment: AgenTracer-8B trained with multi-granular RL on TracerTraj, failed multi-agent trajectories annotated automatically by counterfactual replay and programmed fault injection; evaluated on Who&When against proprietary LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-4-Sonnet); feedback given to the multi-agent systems MetaGPT and MaAS.
findings.bears_on: Reppert item 4 (diagnosis learned by LMs): a lightweight failure tracer trained on automatically annotated failed trajectories outperformed large proprietary LLMs on Who&When by up to 18.18%; the quoted lines do not establish that its absolute accuracy is high enough to replace human analysis.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2512.06749v3: DoVer: Intervention-Driven Auto Debugging for LLM Multi-Agent Systems
findings.claim: The authors argue that log-only LLM failure localization yields untested hypotheses and that single-step or single-agent attribution is often ill-posed because multiple distinct interventions can independently repair a failed task; their intervention-driven debugger (editing messages, altering plans) flipped 18-28% of failed trials into successes and validated or refuted 30-60% of failure hypotheses on GAIA- and AssistantBench-derived data in Magentic-One.
findings.setting: Experiment: Magentic-One multi-agent framework on datasets derived from GAIA and AssistantBench, plus GSMPlus with AG2; evaluation by task success and milestone progress rather than attribution accuracy.
findings.bears_on: Error analysis and repair (items 3-4): proposes intervention-verified hypotheses and outcome-based success, rather than attribution accuracy, as the target for automated debugging.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2603.23994v2: Understanding the Challenges in Iterative Generative Optimization with LLMs
findings.claim: The authors state that generative optimization, which uses LLMs to iteratively improve artifacts such as code, workflows or prompts using execution feedback, remains brittle in practice (only 9% of surveyed agents used any automated optimization). They argue this brittleness arises because setting up a learning loop requires 'hidden' design choices, and through case studies find that three such factors (the starting artifact, the credit horizon for execution traces, and batching trials and errors into learning evidence) can determine whether generative optimization succeeds. They argue the lack of adoption is not a consequence of inadequate infrastructure support or insufficient software abstraction, and conclude that the lack of a simple, universal way to set up learning loops across domains is a major hurdle for productionization and adoption.
findings.setting: Case studies (experiments) with LLM-based generative optimization on MLAgentBench, Atari and BigBench Extra Hard (BBEH); plus a survey figure the authors give (only 9% of surveyed agents used any automated optimization) and their argument, pointing to the ecosystem of agent-building libraries, that low adoption is not due to inadequate infrastructure or software.
findings.bears_on: Reppert items 3-4: the authors argue that a major hurdle for automated LLM-based improvement of code, workflows or prompts is setting up the learning loop rather than missing infrastructure or software; this is an argument plus case studies on benchmarks, not a test of LM-program repair in Reppert et al.'s open-ended setting.

passages.text:
Generative optimization uses large language models (LLMs) to iteratively improve
artifacts (such as code, workflows or prompts) using execution feedback. It is
a promising approach to building self-improving agents, yet in practice remains
brittle: despite active research, only 9% of surveyed agents used any automated

optimization. We argue that this brittleness arises because, to set up a learning
loop, an engineer must make “hidden” design choices: What can the optimizer edit
and what is the “right” learning evidence to provide at each update? We investigate
three factors that affect most applications: the starting artifact, the credit horizon
for execution traces, and batching trials and errors into learning evidence. Through
case studies in MLAgentBench, Atari, and BigBench Extra Hard, we find that these
design decisions can determine whether generative optimization succeeds, yet they
are rarely made explicit in prior work. Different starting artifacts determine which
solutions are reachable in MLAgentBench, truncated traces can still improve Atari
agents, and larger minibatches do not monotonically improve generalization on
BBEH. We conclude that the lack of a simple, universal way to set up learning
loops across domains is a major hurdle for productionization and adoption. We

This lack of adoption is not a consequence of inadequate infrastructure support or insufficient software
abstraction. On the contrary, over the past two years, a rich ecosystem of powerful libraries for
building agentic systems has emerged (Khattab et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024; LangChain, 2024; Cheng
et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). Many of these libraries offer mechanisms for automatically optimizing
different targets, ranging from tuning prompts (Khattab et al., 2024; Yuksekgonul et al., 2025) to
program synthesis (Cheng et al., 2024). Most of them have received considerable attention from
agent engineers, suggesting that the low adoption rate cannot be attributed solely to limited awareness
or inadequate software.
